To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the proposed convolutional neural network architecture is universal to any graph, (2) it can learn local, stationary and compositional features, and (3) it is fast, with linear computational complexity and linear learning complexity, and it can scale to large graphs.
we propose a novel deep learning system for graphs that is universal to any graph, and that has the same computational complexity as classical CNN.
we propose a formulation of CNN on graphs, based on spectral graph theory, and we provide efficient numerical schemes to compute localized convolutional filters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel deep learning methods for graph-structured data
the design of deep learning architectures for the analysis of high dimensional data represented by graphs.
the following question: Can we generalize the convolutional neural network to graphs, while preserving the linear computational and constant learning complexity?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CNNs are not the only way to go.
the authors have developed an effective method for applying convolutional neural networks to graphs, which is a very important contribution.
the proposed CNN architecture is the first one that can be used to learn local, stationnary and compositional features from data represented by graphs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed the first convolutional neural networks that can be applied to arbitrary graphs, and that are as fast as classical CNNs.
we are able to design a convolutional neural network that is universal to any graph topology, and is as fast as a classical CNN.
we propose a generalization of CNNs from low dimensional regular domains to high dimensional irregular ones.

the graph Laplacian can be used to design fast and efficient convolutional filters on irregular domains.
spectral filters are a promising approach to design convolutional neural networks on irregular domains.
